title: Customer firewall SNI rewrite -> control plane stall retrospective
content:
Summary:

Nov 18–19 2026: Several Private/VPC customers reported intermittent control-plane stalls where model servers failed to establish or maintain gRPC connections to the control-plane API (RPCs for allocation, health pings, and config fetch). Impact varied: for most customers it manifested as transient deployment/scale failures and elevated API error rates; for one large on-prem customer it caused ~20m of pod churn and degraded inference availability for traffic routed through a customer-managed firewall appliance.

This doc collects timeline, detection, root-cause hypotheses and final analysis: a customer-side deep-packet-inspection (DPI) proxy running in their firewall had been updated to rewrite SNI for outbound TLS handshakes. The SNI rewrite broke our control-plane TLS routing expectations for mutual TLS and SNI-based routing between customer agents and the control-plane, causing gRPC connections to be routed to an edge proxy that did not support the expected ALPN/gRPC passthrough, resulting in silent resets and long reconnect delays.

Why this is different from prior incidents:
- Not an internal routing bug or capacity exhaustion — the failure surface was in an upstream customer-managed appliance rewriting TLS metadata.
- The symptom set (gRPC stream resets, ALPN mismatch, TLS SNI mismatch) required packet-level inspection and reproduction with the customer firewall in the loop.
- Exposed a blind spot in our mTLS + SNI-based client identity inference when intermediate proxies mutate TLS handshake fields.

High-level impact:
- Customer A (on-prem, large): ~20m service degradation, elevated error rates on control-plane RPCs; some workers restarted because they considered control-plane unreachable.
- Customer B/C (VPC with customer-managed NAT/firewalls): transient failures during policy refreshes; increased retries and fallback to cached policy for up to 10m.
- Internal alerting: SRE observed increased gRPC RESETs and connection churn beginning 2026-11-18 08:52 UTC and spike through 09:15 UTC.

Timeline (key events):
- 2026-11-18 08:45 UTC: First pager (SRE oncall) for increased RPC error rates (internal alert based on percentiles of gRPC success rate).
- 2026-11-18 08:52 UTC: Customer A opens support ticket: agent failing to handshake to control-plane; includes firewall logs showing TLS handshake rewrite event at 08:49.
- 2026-11-18 09:05 UTC: Oncall escalates to Private Deployments and Network SRE. Initial hypothesis: internal edge proxy misconfiguration.
- 2026-11-18 09:13 UTC: Slack thread with Customer Eng (Ruth) and the customer network team. Customer confirms they rolled a DPI signature update at 08:46 that rewrote SNI to canonicalize hostnames for policy grouping.
- 2026-11-18 09:27 UTC: Packet captures from customer environment show SNI set to our public hostname but with an appended token (e.g., redwood-control.example.com -> redwood-control.example.com+fwtag). Our control-plane TLS server rejected the altered handshake (certificate name mismatch and ALPN negotiation failed), and in some edge nodes the request was redirected to a generic TLS-terminating proxy.
- 2026-11-18 09:40 UTC: Short mitigation: customer disabled the DPI SNI rewrite rule; gRPC connections recovered within 2–5 minutes for most agents.
- 2026-11-18 09:55 UTC: Post-mitigation monitoring shows remaining slow reconnects for long-lived connections that experienced repeated resets.

Detection and debugging notes (timeline granular):
- Initial observability signals: gRPC error rate, server-side 14x resets, control-plane API latency SLO violation for allocation RPCs.
- Useful logs/metrics:
  - controlplane.grpc.connections.active (doubling during incident)
  - controlplane.grpc.errors_by_code{code="UNAVAILABLE"} spiked
  - edge-proxy.tls.failures (increase in cert mismatch logs)
  - FW logs from customer: events tagged "sni-rewrite" with rule id and signature version
- Packet capture findings: altered SNI value, ALPN list without h2 in some flows (proxy stripped negotiated ALPN), occasional TLS rehandshakes that failed our client_cert verification.

Root cause analysis:
- Direct cause: Customer-managed DPI/proxy appliance rewrote TLS SNI header for outbound control-plane connections. That rewrite changed the server_name presented in the TLS handshake and in some flows changed/removed ALPN information, which caused (a) our TLS selection logic to present the wrong cert or drop to a TLS-terminating path, (b) gRPC client and server unable to negotiate HTTP/2 (h2) ALPN, leading to connection resets.
- Contributing factors:
  - Our control-plane relies on SNI and mTLS metadata to select TLS contexts and route to the correct backend in edge clusters. We lack a fallback path or robust verification that is tolerant to middlebox SNI mutation.
  - The agent's client-side logging did not surface the ALPN mismatch clearly; it reported generic SSL handshake failure, making initial triage ambiguous.
  - Customers sometimes apply DPI updates during off-hours; policy changes were rolled without coordinated notification to Redwood.

Why the SNI rewrite was applied by the customer:
- The customer's security team uses SNI canonicalization to consolidate policy usage across many services; the DPI signature update added a transform to normalize hostnames. This was intended to help the customer's internal URL grouping and blocklist rules.

Mitigation actions taken during incident: 
- Immediate: recommended customer to disable the new DPI signature and SNI-rewrite rule (done at 09:40 UTC).
- Short-term platform fixes: accepted additional ALPN-handling logs from edge-proxy to make handshakes failures more visible. Rolled a logging change to agents to include TLS ClientHello SNI and ALPN (non-sensitive subset) in debug mode to aid future triage (opt-in).
- Communication: CS & account teams notified customer of recommended firewall configuration and capture we needed. Internal post-incident mailing list created.

Permanent fixes and action items (owner, ETA):
- (PRIORITY) Add explicit detection of mutated SNI/ALPN patterns in edge ingress and raise structured alert (SRE) — owner: Evan Chu — ETA: 2026-11-30.
- Update agent debug logging to include ALPN & SNI on TLS failures (opt-in via debug env) so customers can produce captures without sharing private certs — owner: Miguel Torres — ETA: 2026-12-07.
- Document recommended customer firewall/DPI rules for Private/Onprem deployments (Customer Eng + Solutions) — owner: Ruth P. — ETA: 2026-12-03. Deliverable: one-pager with allowed transformations and example firewall exceptions.
- Runbook: create an SRE runbook entry "If control-plane RPCs fail and gRPC RESETs spike -> check for SNI mutation by customer middlebox" with the following quick checks and sample commands — owner: Aisha Khatri — ETA: 2026-11-25.
- Engineering: explore fallback handshake logic for edge (safe ALPN fallback, explicit reject logs, avoid silent proxying) — owner: eng-serving-runtime team — RFC by 2026-12-15.

Suggested runbook quick-check steps (draft):
1) Check metrics: controlplane.grpc.errors_by_code{code!="OK"} and edge-proxy.tls.failures. If gRPC UNAVAILABLE spikes, proceed.
2) Request packet capture from customer for outbound handshake to control-plane IPs (pcap of 3 minutes). Filter: host <control-plane-ip> and tcp port 443.
3) In capture, inspect ClientHello.server_name and ALPN extension. If server_name contains additional tokens or does not match expected host, flag SNI mutation.
4) Ask customer to temporarily disable DPI signature or add exception for control-plane hosts.
5) If immediate disable not possible, consider short-term rate-limited retry window on agent + extended backoff to avoid thundering reconnect attempts.

PromQL/Alert suggestions to add: (draft snippets)
- Alert: edge-proxy-sni-mutation-suspect:
  expr: increase(edge_proxy_tls_cert_mismatch_total[5m]) > 10 and increase(controlplane_grpc_unavailable_count[5m]) > 30
  severity: page
- Alert: controlplane-grpc-alpn-drop:
  expr: increase(edge_proxy_alpn_not_h2_total[5m]) > 5
  severity: ticket

Notes for customer-facing one-pager (to be produced by Customer Eng):
- Explain SNI importance and how DPI SNI-rewrite can unintentionally break mTLS and ALPN required for gRPC.
- Provide example firewall signature exceptions (by SNI or destination IP/port) and recommended ordering of DPI rules.
- Provide a minimal debug checklist they can run before contacting support (capture commands: tcpdump -w /tmp/ctrl.pcap port 443 and grep ClientHello patterns).

Open questions / discussion points:
- Should we stop depending on SNI for backend selection where mTLS is present? Pros/cons.
- Can we add a lightweight in-band handshake probe (non-sensitive) so the agent can detect and report SNI/ALPN mutation without exposing cert material?
- What SLAs or guidance should we require for customers who run middleboxes that alter TLS metadata?

Appendix: quick reproduction steps used with customer (notes):
- Customer provided a test sandbox with the same DPI appliance. We reproduced by enabling their SNI rewrite rule and replaying an agent bootup that opens gRPC channels. Observed: TLS ClientHello SNI mutated and ALPN list trimmed; server chose a generic cert and upstream rejected h2 negotiation -> connection resets.
- Example tcpdump excerpt (hex-decoded form) showed ClientHello server_name: "redwood-control.example.com+norm-v2".

Post-incident follow-ups scheduled:
- 2026-11-22 15:00 UTC: Cross-team (SRE, Serving Runtime, Customer Eng) retro to finalize runbook text and prioritize RFC.
- 2026-12-06: Customer-eng deliver one-pager and example firewall configs to Customer A and publish to private-deployments onboarding docs.

Notes-to-self / rough TODOs (incomplete):
- Add a small code snippet to agent docs that explains how to collect ClientHello SNI safely (no certs).
- Confirm whether Load Balancer in front of edge preserves original SNI after TLS passthrough; if not, update architecture doc.
- Track SRE-4712 and close only after alerts + runbook + docs are merged.

——END——

This is draft-internal: aim is to capture incident context and create a concise runbook so future SRE oncall can quickly identify customer-side SNI mutations as a root cause for control-plane gRPC failures.
